blocks.text: Disappointed, K. took the letter and put it into his pocket. Even in the most favorable case, the advantage that the recommendation might bring him was comparatively smaller than the damage that lay in the fact that the manufacturer knew of his trial and that the painter was spreading the news further. He could scarcely force himself to thank the manufacturer, who was already on his way to the door, with a few words. "I shall go there," he said, as he took leave of the manufacturer at the door, "or, since I am very busy at present, write to him that he might come to me at the office sometime." "I knew, after all," said the manufacturer, "that you would find the best way out. To be sure, I thought that you would rather avoid inviting people like this Titorelli into the bank in order to speak with him here about the trial. Nor is it always advantageous to let letters to such people out of one's hands. But you have certainly thought everything through and know what you may do." K. nodded and accompanied the manufacturer further through the anteroom. Yet despite his outward calm he was very much alarmed at himself. That he would write to Titorelli he had really only said in order to show the manufacturer in some way that he knew how to appreciate the recommendation and was immediately considering the possibilities of meeting with Titorelli, yet if he had regarded Titorelli's assistance as valuable, he would not have hesitated to write to him in earnest either. The dangers, however, that could result from this he had only recognized through the manufacturer's remark. Could he indeed already rely so little upon his own judgment? If it was possible that he should invite a questionable person into the bank by means of an explicit letter in order to ask him, separated only by a door from the Deputy Director, for advice regarding his trial, was it not then possible and even very probable that he was also overlooking other dangers or running straight into them? There was not always someone standing beside him to warn him. And precisely now, when he wanted to act with all his gathered strength, such doubts about his own vigilance, hitherto foreign to him, had to arise! Were the difficulties that he felt in carrying out his office work now to begin in the trial as well? Now, to be sure, he no longer understood at all how it had been possible that he had wanted to write to Titorelli and invite him into the bank.

He was still shaking his head over it when the attendant stepped to his side and drew his attention to three gentlemen who were sitting on a bench here in the anteroom. They had already been waiting a long time to be admitted to K. Now, as the attendant was speaking with K., they had stood up and each wanted to seize a favorable opportunity to approach K. ahead of the others. Since the bank had been so inconsiderate as to let them waste their time here in the waiting room, they too did not wish to exercise any further consideration. "Mr. Chief Clerk," one of them was already saying. But K. had had the attendant bring his winter coat and, while he put it on with the attendant's help, said to all three: "Forgive me, gentlemen, I unfortunately have no time at this moment to receive you. I beg your pardon most sincerely, but I have an urgent business errand to attend to and must leave at once. You have seen for yourselves, after all, how long I have just been detained. Would you be so kind as to come back tomorrow or whenever you like? Or shall we perhaps discuss the matters by telephone? Or would you perhaps like to tell me briefly now what it is about, and I will then give you a detailed written reply. It would be best, to be sure, if you came some other time soon." These proposals of K.'s threw the gentlemen, who were now supposed to have waited completely in vain, into such astonishment that they looked at one another in silence. "We are agreed, then?" asked K., who had turned toward the attendant, who was now bringing him his hat as well. Through the open door to K.'s room one could see how the snowfall outside had grown much heavier. K. therefore turned up his coat collar and buttoned it high under his throat.
